quotes.text: The appellant was prosecuted for committing 8 offences punishable u/s 302/34 IPC read with s.314 of TADA in connection with the death of a doctor, who was shot dead in his clinic while attending the patients.

A doctor shot dead by two miscreants in his clinic - Deceased's daughter, who was eye-witness and wife who was slightly away from scene of occurrence, not examined - Held: Both the wife and the daughter of deceased are the most natural and competent witnesses.

The trial court has placed reliance on the evidence of a witness who has come forward for recording his statement u!s 161 CrPC almost after two years and eight months - The only explanation he has given is that he was threatened by the co-accused - Six years after his statement was recorded, accused was arrested - The plea of threat to keep him silent for almost two years and eight months does not inspire confidence - His testimony is thoroughly and wholly unreliable.

trial_court_outcome.value: Convicted under IPC s.302, acquitted under TADA

quotes.text: The Designated Court acquitted him of the offences under the Terrorist and Disruptive Activities (Prevention) Act, 1987, but convicted and sentenced him to imprisonment for life uls 302 IPC.

Allowing the appeal, the Court HELD: 1.1. There is no dispute over the fact that the deceased was fired from the point blank range, as is evident from the post mortem report. Therefore, the death is homicidal, is beyond doubt.

neutral_facts.value: The accused, a man, was involved in the shooting death of a doctor, who was shot dead in his clinic while attending to patients. The deceased was shot from point blank range, as confirmed by the post mortem report. The prosecution relied on the testimony of a witness, PW-14, who came forward almost two years and eight months after the incident. The witness claimed to be threatened by the co-accused, but the delay in his statement and the lack of corroboration raised doubts about his reliability. The prosecution also failed to examine the deceased's wife and daughter, who were present at the scene and could have provided crucial evidence. The trial court convicted the accused under IPC s.302 based on the testimony of PW-14, but the High Court and Supreme Court found the evidence insufficient and set aside the conviction.

quotes.text: An FIR was lodged by one Kumud Bora on the following day i.e. 3.3.1991 at Jamuguri police station under Sonitpur district and on the basis of the said FIR Station Case No. 20/91 u/s 302/34 IPC read with Sections 3/4 of TADA was registered which set the criminal law in motion.

procedural_irregularity.value: Non-examination of material witnesses (wife and daughter of the deceased) which affected the prosecution case.

quotes.text: Both the wife and the daughter of deceased are the most natural and competent witnesses. They really could have thrown immense light on the factual score, but, they have not been examined.

appeal_history.value: Trial court: Convicted under Section 302 IPC. High Court: Acquitted under TADA but convicted under Section 302 IPC. Supreme Court: Appeal allowed, conviction set aside.

quotes.text: The judgment of conviction is set aside. The appellant was prosecuted for committing 8 offences punishable u/s 302/34 IPC read with s.314 of TADA in connection with the death of a doctor, who was shot dead in his clinic while attending the patients.

prosecution_argument.value: The prosecution argued that the deceased was shot dead by two unidentified youths from the point blank range, and that the accused-appellant was involved in the crime. They relied on the testimony of PW-14, who claimed to be the eye-witness, and the post-mortem report indicating the cause of death was due to shock and hemorrhage from bullet injuries.

quotes.text: The prosecution case, as unfolded, is that on 2.3.1991 about 6.30 p.m., the deceased, Dr. Swapan Sathi Barman, a medical practitioner, while attending to the patients in his clinic, was shot by two unidentified youths from the point blank range as a consequence of which he breathed his last.

defence_argument.value: The defence argued that the sole witness, PW-14, was unreliable due to his delayed statement and the lack of corroboration. They also highlighted the non-examination of the deceased's wife and daughter, who were natural witnesses, and contended that the prosecution's failure to examine them created a dent in their case.

quotes.text: The defence chose not to adduce any evidence. The Designated Court did not find any material to show complicity of the accused in any of the offences in respect of which charges had been framed under the TADA and accordingly opined that he was not guilty of the same.

legal_principle_applied.value: The Supreme Court applied the principle that conviction can be based on the testimony of a single witness provided he is wholly reliable, but if there are doubts about the testimony, the courts will insist on corroboration. The court also emphasized the importance of examining material witnesses and the consequences of their non-examination.

quotes.text: It is well settled in law that conviction can be based on the testimony of a singular witness. It has been held in Sunil Kumar** that as a general rule the court can and may act on the testimony of a single witness provided he is wholly reliable.
